guidance: Security aid—validate the result in a controlled environment and against current authoritative guidance before protecting a real system or secret.
method: The requested redirect_uri is parsed into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment, and is refused when it is not an absolute URI with a scheme, when it carries a fragment, a space, a control character, a non-numeric port, or no host or path at all; RFC 6749 section 3.1.2 requires an absolute URI and forbids the fragment. Each registered URI is trimmed from its line and checked the same way, but a bad line is skipped and counted rather than failing the whole list, so one stale console entry does not hide a working one. With a fully registered URI the comparison is simple string comparison as RFC 6749 section 3.1.2.3 directs through RFC 3986 section 6.2.1, which is why nothing is normalised: scheme and host case, percent-encoding, a default port written out, a trailing slash and the order of query parameters are all part of the value. When only the scheme, authority and path are registered (section 3.1.2.2), those three components are compared as written and the query may vary, except that an entry which itself carries a query pins it. A loopback redirect on http may use any port: RFC 8252 section 7.3 requires the authorization server to allow whatever ephemeral port the native app is listening on, for the 127.0.0.1 and [::1] IP literals, while path and query must still match; the localhost hostname is compared literally because the exception is written for the IP literal. When nothing matches, the closest entry is the one differing in the fewest components, and the first differing component is reported with both values, in the order scheme, host, port, path, query. An entry containing an asterisk is compared literally like any other string, so it can never match a real URI and is called out rather than treated as a wildcard. Notes cover plain http (RFC 6749 section 3.1.2.1 prefers TLS), credentials in the authority, a private-use scheme registered for a web client (RFC 8252 section 7.1 reserves those for native apps) and duplicate entries. The check models the comparison, not a provider: registration consoles can normalise a value on save, some providers accept a subdomain wildcard or an extra-query allowlist, and neither PKCE, state nor the rest of the authorization request is evaluated. Inputs allow up to 50 registered URIs and a redirect_uri of at most 4,096 characters, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
